implementation_notes: Boost.Serialization replaces the hand-written graph walk: give each class a serialize() member (or an ADL free function) and stream the whole graph through an archive, then bind the resulting bytes as BYTEA/BLOB. Declare class versions (BOOST_CLASS_VERSION plus version-aware serialize()) or archives become unreadable after a field change. The archive is a private Boost format, so read it back only from trusted data, and prefer it when the payload stays inside one C++ service.
pitfalls: Without BOOST_CLASS_VERSION and a version-aware serialize(), adding a field makes every archived blob unreadable or silently mis-parsed.
Shared pointers and cycles need Boost's pointer-tracking support (shared_ptr/weak_ptr serialization) or the graph is duplicated or lost on the way back.
Boost archives are not a security boundary: do not load archives that may have been tampered with, and never from untrusted sources.

variants.name: nlohmann/json text in a JSON/TEXT column
variants.implementation_notes: Free to_json/from_json functions found by ADL give the library its hook, so the graph becomes JSON text that can live in a TEXT/JSONB column and be inspected with SQL. Unknown members are ignored on read, which buys forward compatibility at the price of silently ignoring typos, and the payload is human-readable, which shortens debugging and lets other services read it.
pitfalls: j.at() throws on a missing field while j[key] inserts null: choosing the wrong accessor turns a schema change into either a crash or a quietly wrong graph.
A deeply nested graph stresses the recursive parser and dumper; bound the depth or the payload size at the storage boundary.

variants.name: Protocol Buffers schema-first blob
variants.idiom_name: generated protobuf message + SerializeToString() into BYTEA
variants.implementation_notes: A .proto schema plus generated C++ classes replace both mapper and serializer: SerializeToString()/ParseFromString() own the encoding, unknown fields survive for forward compatibility and the payload is language-neutral, so sibling services can read it. Adds a protoc build step and forces the graph into messages, so prefer it when several languages or long-lived data are involved.
pitfalls: Field numbers are the contract: reusing a retired number silently mis-reads old blobs, so removed fields must be reserved.
ParseFromString returns false on malformed input and leaves a partially populated message; check the result before building the graph.
